title: Write a commit message people can use

scenario.brief:
**Where you are.** Your friend Priya looked at your history and said the last message, `stuff`, tells her nothing. She is right. You will fix it, then write a proper message for a new change.

**The rules teams use.** A good message has a short first line, like a headline, written as an instruction: "Add salt to recipe", not "added salt" or "salt." Keep it under 50 characters if you can, never over 72, and do not end it with a full stop. If you need to explain *why*, leave one empty line and write a sentence or two after it.

**What you'll do.**

1. Look at the bad message: `git log --oneline`.
2. Replace the latest message without changing the files: `git commit --amend -m "Add cooking time to pancake recipe"`. Amend means "rewrite the latest commit".
3. Make a new change: open `recipe.md`, add a line `Serves: 2`, save.
4. Commit it with a headline **and** a body. Type `git commit -am "Add serving size to recipe" -m "Priya asked how many people the recipe feeds."` The first `-m` is the headline, the second becomes the body after a blank line.
5. Check with `git log`. Two tidy messages at the top.
scenario.whyItMatters: Six months from now, a message is often the only explanation of why a line exists. Teams reject pull requests with messages like "fix" or "stuff".

objectives.title: Replace the message "stuff" with a clear headline
objectives.description: Same files, better message, under 72 characters, no full stop at the end.
hints: You can rewrite the most recent commit's message. Nobody else has this history, so it is safe.
`git commit --amend -m "New message"` replaces the latest commit with the same files and a new message.
Type: `git commit --amend -m "Add cooking time to pancake recipe"`

objectives.title: Commit a new change with a headline and a body
objectives.description: Add `Serves: 2` to recipe.md, then commit with a first line and an explanation after a blank line.
hints: Edit recipe.md (click it, or `code recipe.md`), add a line `Serves: 2`, save with Ctrl+S.
Two `-m` flags make a headline and a body: the first is the first line, the second goes after a blank line. `-a` stages every tracked file that changed.
Type: `git commit -am "Add serving size to recipe" -m "Priya asked how many people the recipe feeds."`

debrief.summary: You repaired a useless message and wrote one with a headline and a reason. Your history now reads like a story.
internals: `--amend` did not edit the old commit; it created a new one with the same files and a new message and moved the branch to it. The old one is simply no longer in the chain.
A commit message is stored as plain text. The first line is the subject; tools like `git log --oneline` show only that line, which is why it must stand alone.
The blank line separates subject from body so Git and every tool can tell them apart.

keyCommands.note: Rewrite the latest commit's message. Only for commits you have not shared yet.
Stage every tracked change and commit in one go. Does not add new files.

commonMistakes: Amending a commit that teammates already have. That rewrites shared history and causes confusion; later tracks cover the rule.
Messages in past tense or with a full stop: "Added salt." Write "Add salt".
Explaining *what* in the body when the diff already shows it. The body is for *why*.
debrief.atWork: Many teams enforce these rules automatically and refuse commits that break them. Good messages make code review, changelogs and bug hunting faster for everyone.
debrief.interview: "What makes a good commit message?" Answer: a short imperative subject, a blank line, and a body that explains why.

solution: git commit --amend -m "Add cooking time to pancake recipe"
git commit -am "Add serving size to recipe" -m "Priya asked how many people the recipe feeds."
